name: Sepsis & Infection
sub: Sepsis-3, SSC, antimicrobials, tropical fevers, CNS and soft-tissue infection

cards.q: Define sepsis and septic shock (Sepsis-3).
cards.a: Sepsis: life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection (SOFA increase ≥2). Septic shock: vasopressors needed for MAP ≥65 mmHg and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluids.

cards.q: What does the Surviving Sepsis Campaign say about antibiotic timing?
cards.a: Septic shock, or probable/definite sepsis without shock: give antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 hour of recognition (strong). Possible sepsis without shock: brief rapid work-up, then antimicrobials within 3 hours of first suspicion if infection is still suspected (conditional). If infection is unlikely, defer antibiotics and monitor closely.

cards.q: When should blood cultures be taken?
cards.a: As soon as possible and ideally before antimicrobials (strong), without meaningfully delaying treatment (SSC 2021 used about 45 minutes). Take two sets from different sites, and one from each lumen of any central line.

cards.q: How quickly should source control be achieved?
cards.a: Rapidly evaluate every patient for a source needing control. SSC 2026 suggests early source control, ideally within 6 hours of diagnosis (conditional), for drainable or removable sources: abscess, infected device, necrotising infection, obstructed system.

cards.q: What biomarker supports stopping antibiotics earlier?
cards.a: Procalcitonin plus clinical evaluation can help decide when to stop when duration is unclear (SSC 2026, conditional). Sepsis is a clinical diagnosis: do not start or withhold antibiotics on procalcitonin alone.

cards.q: What is a standard empirical regimen for severe community-acquired pneumonia?
cards.a: A beta-lactam (e.g. ceftriaxone) plus a macrolide (or a respiratory fluoroquinolone), adding anti-pseudomonal or anti-MRSA cover when risk factors exist. Duration is usually 5–7 days if responding. ATS 2025 suggests systemic corticosteroids for hospitalised severe CAP (conditional, low-quality evidence; not for influenza pneumonia) and allows non-severe CAP that improves within 3 days to stop after a minimum of 3 days.

cards.q: When is anti-MRSA therapy added and which drugs are used?
cards.a: In suspected MRSA infection (known colonisation, prior MRSA infection, skin and soft tissue or line sepsis, cavitating pneumonia): vancomycin (AUC/MIC 400–600) or linezolid.

cards.q: Which treatment is first-line for invasive candidiasis in the ICU?
cards.a: An echinocandin (caspofungin, micafungin or anidulafungin); step down to fluconazole if susceptible and stable. Remove or replace central lines.

cards.q: How is C. difficile infection treated?
cards.a: Fidaxomicin 200 mg twice daily for 10 days (preferred) or oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days. Fulminant disease: vancomycin 500 mg four times daily plus IV metronidazole; consider surgery.

cards.q: What are the empiric treatments and adjunct for adult bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV twice daily plus vancomycin; add ampicillin if age >50 or immunocompromised (Listeria). Give dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg every 6 hours for 4 days, started with or before the first antibiotic dose.

cards.q: How is necrotising soft-tissue infection managed?
cards.a: Urgent surgical debridement (do not delay for imaging), broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin (to suppress toxin production) and organ support.

cards.q: What is the antimalarial treatment for severe falciparum malaria?
cards.a: IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 hours, then once daily until oral therapy is possible, followed by a full course of an artemisinin-based combination.

cards.q: When do dengue patients enter the critical phase and which warning signs matter?
cards.a: Usually days 3–7 around defervescence. Warning signs: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, liver enlargement, rising haematocrit with a rapid fall in platelets.
cards.src: WHO dengue guidelines (WHO 2009; a newer WHO arboviral clinical-management guideline was issued in 2025, reviewer to confirm)

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for scrub typhus and leptospirosis?
cards.a: Scrub typhus: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily (azithromycin if unable). Leptospirosis: benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone for severe disease, or doxycycline for milder disease.

cards.q: How do you treat enteric fever in a critically ill patient?
cards.a: Ceftriaxone (with or without azithromycin); consider resistance patterns locally; watch for intestinal perforation and haemorrhage.

cards.q: Define a central-line associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) and the key action.
cards.a: A laboratory-confirmed bloodstream infection with a central line in place for more than 2 days that is not related to infection at another site. Remove the line when possible and treat according to the organism.

cards.q: What infection control precautions apply to C. difficile versus MRSA?
cards.a: C. difficile: contact (enteric) precautions with soap-and-water hand washing, as alcohol gel does not kill spores. MRSA and CRE: contact precautions, with alcohol rub acceptable. TB, measles, varicella: airborne precautions.

cards.q: Give the suggested approach to antibiotic de-escalation.
cards.a: Once a pathogen is confirmed, narrow to the most targeted effective agent (strong); when cultures are negative, de-escalation is suggested (conditional). Review at 48–72 hours, stop if infection is excluded, and choose the shortest effective duration, which SSC 2026 suggests can be shorter with adequate source control.

cards.q: What is the usual duration of antibiotics in uncomplicated Gram-negative bacteraemia?
cards.a: 7 days is as effective as 14 days in patients who improve promptly with source control (Yahav 2019).

cards.q: A 72-year-old has fever, hypotension (BP 78/40), lactate 4.8 and a likely urinary source. What is the best immediate management?
o: Blood cultures, antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid, norepinephrine to MAP ≥65 and source control
Wait for culture results before antibiotics
Give furosemide to prevent pulmonary oedema
cards.e: Septic shock demands rapid antimicrobials, fluid resuscitation and vasopressor support, with early source assessment. SSC 2026 still suggests at least 30 mL/kg crystalloid in the first 3 hours, now with more caveats: individualise and reassess frequently.

cards.q: Which is a typical feature of the dengue critical phase?
o: Plasma leakage with rising haematocrit and falling platelets around defervescence
High fever persisting from day 1 to day 3 only
cards.e: The critical phase begins when fever settles, bringing capillary leak, shock and bleeding. Eschar suggests scrub typhus.

cards.q: How do you give vancomycin in an adult ICU patient?
cards.a: A loading dose of 20–35 mg/kg (actual weight, capped), then maintenance guided by AUC/MIC 400–600 mg·h/L where possible; adjust to renal function and monitor for nephrotoxicity, particularly with piperacillin-tazobactam.

cards.q: Which screening tools does SSC 2026 prefer over qSOFA?
cards.a: NEWS/NEWS2, MEWS or SIRS rather than qSOFA alone for screening acutely ill hospitalised adults (conditional). Sepsis remains a clinical diagnosis; no single biomarker rules it in or out.

cards.q: What does SSC 2026 say about fluids after the initial resuscitation?
cards.a: It suggests active fluid removal (diuretics or ultrafiltration) after the acute resuscitation phase in septic shock, and dynamic measures over static ones or examination alone to guide fluids. Do not keep giving fluid just to normalise lactate. Liberal versus restrictive fluids after the first 30 mL/kg can follow patient and system factors.

cards.q: Which adjuncts does SSC 2026 advise against, and where may vasopressors be started?
cards.a: It suggests against IV vitamin C and against vitamin D for sepsis treatment. Vasopressors may be started peripherally rather than waiting for central access (conditional). After a loading dose, maintenance beta-lactams are given as a prolonged infusion rather than bolus (strong).

cards.q: What are the new prehospital recommendations in SSC 2026?
cards.a: Screen for sepsis en route to hospital, and consider giving antibiotics en route only in select circumstances, such as hypotension with a prolonged transport time (conditional recommendations aimed at speeding diagnosis and treatment).

cards.q: What does the 2025 ATS CAP guideline say about corticosteroids and lung ultrasound?
cards.a: It suggests systemic corticosteroids for hospitalised adults with severe CAP (conditional, low-quality evidence; excludes influenza pneumonia) and recommends against them in non-severe CAP. Lung ultrasound is accepted as a reasonable alternative to chest radiography in suspected CAP.
